title: What should you ask first in a product metric drop case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a product metric drop case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first how the metric is measured, since when it has fallen, and whether the drop was sudden or gradual, because those three facts rule out most explanations before you guess at any. The trap is guessing a cause before you have segmented the drop by region, device and type of user.
body:
The first question to ask

How is the number measured, when did it start falling, and was the drop sudden or gradual?

Measurement comes first because some drops are not real: a tracking change, a new definition or a broken dashboard can make a healthy product look sick. Timing comes next. A sudden overnight fall usually points to something that changed on a date, such as a release, an outage or a price change. A slow decline over months points to competition, product fit or seasonality.

How to build your structure

  1. Check how the number is measured, and whether the drop shows up in other data too.
  2. Establish timing: sudden or gradual, and since when.
  3. Consider external causes (season, holidays, competitors, news) and internal ones (releases, bugs, prices, marketing changes).
  4. Segment the drop by region, platform, app version and new versus returning users.
  5. Form a hypothesis and say how you would test it.

Diagnose a sudden fall without guessing

A food-delivery app's completed orders fell 15% overnight. First, is it real? Check whether payments and restaurant receipts fell too, or only the tracked events. Say they did: the drop is real.

Next, split the metric: completed orders = sessions × conversion. Sessions held at 100,000 a day, but conversion fell from 20% to 17%, so orders fell from 20,000 to 17,000. People are still opening the app; something stops them ordering.

Now segment by platform:

PlatformSessionsConversion before → afterOrders before → after
Android60,00020% → 15%12,000 → 9,000
iOS40,00020% → 20%8,000 → 8,000
Total100,00020% → 17%20,000 → 17,000

The whole drop is on Android. If an Android release went out the evening before, you have a strong lead. Check payment failures, crashes and checkout errors on the new version against the old one. With an average order of $30, the 3,000 lost orders cost about $90k of order value a day, which makes a quick rollback worth considering while the team confirms the cause. Matching timing is not proof, so compare users on the old and new app version before declaring it solved, and say what you would monitor to confirm recovery.

The trap most people fall into

Guessing before segmenting. "Maybe a competitor launched a promotion" may be true, but it would hit both platforms. Splitting first narrows the search in minutes.

Weak: "Orders probably fell because a competitor is running discounts, so we should match them."
Strong: "Before guessing, I'd check the data is right, then split the drop by platform, region and new versus returning users. If it's only Android since Tuesday's release, I'd look at checkout errors on that version first."

Two prompts to try

Average watch time per user on a video app fell 10% over the past three months.

Show the answer
  • Measurement: any change to how watch time is counted, such as autoplay or background play.
  • Mix: are more new or casual users joining, pulling the average down while heavy users are unchanged?
  • External: season, a rival's hit show, fewer new releases.
  • Internal: recommendation changes, more ads, content leaving the catalogue.

Where to start: mix. A gradual fall in an average often means the user base changed, not behaviour.

The trap: looking for a single bug in a gradual decline.

New sign-ups to a banking app dropped 25% in one week.

Show the answer
  • Measurement: tracking or definition changes; does the fall show in accounts opened?
  • Funnel: app downloads, starts of sign-up, identity checks passed, accounts opened.
  • Segments: marketing channel, platform, country.
  • Changes: paused campaigns, a new identity-check supplier, app store ranking.

Where to start: the funnel. Find the step where the fall begins: fewer downloads means marketing; more failed checks means the product.

The trap: blaming marketing before checking the sign-up funnel.
